L149: The investment distribution by customers in Figure 【82†2】(b) resembles a long-tail distribution, where a majority of customers only modify their portfolios a few times over the whole period (over 50% of the users have 3 or less transactions between 2018 and 2022) whereas only a few customers modify their investments continuously (around 650 customers have more than 100 transactions). This long-tail distribution is similar to other recommender system datasets like MovieLens.
L150: A different pattern is observed when we examine the asset distribution however. First, as indicated in Table 【79†1】, less than half of the assets (321 out of 807) have ever been bought or sold in our dataset.
L151: Second, although the distribution illustrated in Figure 【82†2】 is skewed, this is due to a few assets concentrating lots of transactions: even when most of the interacted assets have a reasonable number of transactions (75% of them have more than 20 interactions, and 58% of them have more than 100), the top 12 assets concentrate more than 50% of the dataset interactions. This indicates that there is an important popularity factor over the collected transactions.
L152: ### 3.4 Customers
L153: Financial asset recommendation needs to consider the specific needs and preferences of the customers. However, all that information is not only hidden in the past customer transactions: explicit information about customer investment capacity or risk profile can be considered to identify more relevant investment opportunities for retail customers. As such, we include in the dataset information about the classification of customers within the bank, their investment risk profile and their investment capacity.
L154: We collect that information from the 29,090 customers within the bank who have, at least, one investment reflected in our cleaned transaction data. All customer information has been thoroughly anonymized and does not contain sensitive data to satisfy regulations. We provide further descriptions for the customer classifications below:
L155:  |  |
L156: (a) Customer classification by segment  | (b) Customer classification by risk profile  | (c) Customer classification by capacity
L157: Figure 3: Customer statistics.
L158: #### 3.4.1 Customer segments
L159: 
L160: Customer segments represent the internal classification of customers within the bank. We consider five different segments in our data:
L161: 
L162:   * •
L163: 
L164: Mass: The majority of the customers. This category represents customers with less than €60,000 of managed assets (investments, deposits and insurance products).
L165: 
L166:   * •
L167: 
L168: Premium: Individual customers with more than €60,000 on managed assets.
L169: 
L170:   * •
L250: nDCG@k: We measure how close the recommendations are to the investments made by customers in the $(t,t+\Delta t)$ period using the normalised cumulative discounted gain (nDCG) metric 【86†Järvelin and Kekäläinen (2002)】 over the top $k$ recommendations. It prioritizes relevant assets (i.e. assets acquired during the test period) in the top ranks. We consider that an asset is relevant only if $u$ acquires $i$ during the $(t,t+\Delta t)$ period.
L251: For both metrics, we use $k=10$ and $\Delta t$ equal to six months.
L252: #### 5.2.3 Algorithms
L253: 
L254: To provide a meaningful comparison of evaluation methods, we need to apply these methods over a range of different FAR approaches, hence, we implement a diverse suite of 11 FAR approaches from the literature, summarized below:
L255: 
L256:   * •
L257: 
L258: Random recommendation: As a sanity-check baseline, we include an algorithm recommending assets randomly to customers.
L259: 
L260:   * •
L261: Profitability-based models: We test three regression algorithms, predicting ROI at $t+6$ months: linear regression, random forest and LightGBM regression 【87†Ke et al. (2017)】.
L262: We craft a selection of technical indicators based on close price as features: average price, return on investment, volatility, moving average convergence divergence, momentum, rate of change, relative strength index, detrended close oscillator, return on investment/volatility ratio, and maximum and minimum values over a time period prior to prediction.
L263:   * •
L264: 
L265: Transaction-based models: We choose several methods exploiting investment transactions to generate recommendations. We divide them in two categories:
L266: 
L267:     * –
L268: 
L269: Non-personalized: As a baseline, we consider popularity-based recommendation, which ranks assets according to the number of times they have been purchased in the past.
L270: 
L271:     * –
L272: Collaborative filtering: As collaborative filtering methods, we test three proposals: LightGCN 【88†He et al. (2020)】, matrix factorization (MF) 【89†Rendle et al. (2020)】 and user-based kNN (UB kNN) 【90†Nikolakopoulos et al. (2022)】. We also add the Apriori association rule mining (ARM) algorithm 【91†Agrawal and Srikant (1994)】.
L273: 
L274:   * •
L275: Hybrid methods: Finally, we test two hybrid methods, based on gradient boosting regression trees 【87†Ke et al. (2017)】; 【37†Sanz-Cruzado et al. (2022)】: a regression LightGBM algorithm, targeting the profitability at six months in the future (Hybrid-regression), and, second, the LightGBM implementation of the LambdaMART learning to rank algorithm 【92†Burges (2010)】, optimizing nDCG (Hybrid-nDCG). As features, we use the outcome of all the previous listed recommendation algorithms.
L276: For each algorithm, we select as the optimal hyperparameters those maximizing the ROI at 6 months at three dates: April 1st 2019, October 1st 2019 and January 31st 2020.
L277: ### 5.3 Experimental results
L278: In order to foster research over this dataset, we provide a benchmark of multiple FAR models on the dataset. We therefore report the performance of the 11 FAR approaches in Table 【93†2】 where every column represents one evaluation metric averaged over all the considered time points. The highest performing model under each metric is highlighted in bold and underlined, and the performance distribution for each metric is colour coded (blue for highly performing and red for poorly performing).
L279: From Table 【93†2】 we observe the following points of interest:
L280: Table 2: Effectiveness of the compared models at cutoff 10. A cell color goes from red (lower) to blue (higher values) for each metric, with the top value both underlined and highlighted in bold. For ROI, blue cells show an improvement over the average market value.

L282: None  | Random  | 0.0106  | 0.0071
L283: Prices  | Random forest  | 0.0237  | 0.0259

L295: First, we observe that, in general, only a few of the algorithms are able to provide a set of assets which are profitable above the market ($\mbox{ROI}@10>0.0079$): the price-based algorithms, the hybrid model optimizing a profitability regression function and the user-based kNN collaborative filtering algorithm.
L296: Among these, the best alternatives are notably the profitability prediction models, with the three of them (linear regression, random forest and LightGBM) being able to beat the monthly profitability of a market fund where all assets are equally weighted. From these three models, random forest regression appears as the best alternative. However, these methods fail to identify assets on which customers are interested (achieving nDCG values barely above random recommendation).
L297: Second, transaction-based algorithms are able to reasonably predict customer preferences (as shown by their high nDCG values). We observe that the algorithm with the highest nDCG value is the most advanced LightGCN algorithm. However, we can also notice that the rest of the approaches tested are not able to outperform the non-personalized popularity-based recommendation algorithm. This follows our previous observation that 10 assets concentrate around 50% of the investment transactions in our dataset.
L298: Although collaborative filtering approaches achieve high nDCG values in our comparison, they show an overall poor performance in terms of the ROI profitability metric.
L299: These observations allow us to answer RQ1 and RQ2: those methods targeting a particular evaluation objective are the best optimizing that perspective at evaluation time, with price-based methods like random forest or LightGBM achieving high profitability values, whereas collaborative filtering transaction-based approaches like LightGCN stand out against other algorithms in terms of nDCG.
L300: ## 6 Conclusions
L301: 
L302: In this work, we have introduced FAR-Trans, a novel dataset for financial asset recommendation that includes customer and asset information, asset pricing time series and investment transaction data from a large financial institution. The dataset spans the period between January 2018 and November 2022, covering not only bullish periods, but also periods of time impacted by external events such as the Covid-19 pandemic or the Ukraine-Russia war.
L303: We also compare 11 recommendation algorithms in terms of their capability for recommending profitable assets and their capacity for predicting future customer investments. We find that the non-personalized profitability prediction algorithms are more capable of navigating the market prices and are therefore able to provide asset recommendations above the average market profitability. On the other hand, they fail at predicting customer investments, a task on which collaborative filtering models excel.
L304: As future work, we shall explore the use of this dataset for multiple tasks, not only including financial asset recommendation, but also portfolio construction and optimisation or investor and asset modelling.

L15: > Abstract:Most recommendation benchmarks evaluate how well a model imitates user behavior. In financial advisory, however, observed actions can be noisy or short-sighted under market volatility and may conflict with a user's long-term goals. Treating what users chose as the sole ground truth, therefore, conflates behavioral imitation with decision quality. We introduce Conv-FinRe, a conversational and longitudinal benchmark for stock recommendation that evaluates LLMs beyond behavior matching.
L16: Given an onboarding interview, step-wise market context, and advisory dialogues, models must generate rankings over a fixed investment horizon. Crucially, Conv-FinRe provides multi-view references that distinguish descriptive behavior from normative utility grounded in investor-specific risk preferences, enabling diagnosis of whether an LLM follows rational analysis, mimics user noise, or is driven by market momentum.
L17: We build the benchmark from real market data and human decision trajectories, instantiate controlled advisory conversations, and evaluate a suite of state-of-the-art LLMs. Results reveal a persistent tension between rational decision quality and behavioral alignment: models that perform well on utility-based ranking often fail to match user choices, whereas behaviorally aligned models can overfit short-term noise. The dataset is publicly released on Hugging Face, and the codebase is available on GitHub.

L241: ### 6.4. Federated Client Simulation
L242: 
L243: We simulate 20 clients representing financial institutions. Clients are defined based on three user-level attributes available in the FAR-Trans dataset (【39†Sanz-Cruzado et al., 2024】):

This results in realistic behavioral skew (e.g., some clients serving mostly conservative, low-capacity customers). L257: Across all clients, we generate 23,784 labeled prompt-completion examples for KTO fine-tuning, evenly split between desirable and undesirable completions.
L258: ### 6.5. Model Configurations and Training Protocol
L259: 
L260: We use various sizes of the Qwen3 model (0.6B, 1.7B, 4B, and 8B) (【60†Face, 2024】). The 8B model is excluded from FL due to compute constraints. These models usually have a context length of 32,768 tokens, but we use yarn (【68†Peng et al., 2023】) to increase it to 131,072.
L261: For fine-tuning, we use LoRA (【62†Hu et al., 2022】) with a rank of 16 and alpha of 64. The rank controls the size of the LoRA adaptations, and we choose a rank of 16 because it provides enough new parameters to work with while keeping the fine-tuning lightweight. Short Purchase Histories in FAR-Trans
Student Neklyudov Vladislav Team VibeCoding Team 7
Email vsneklyudov@edu.hse.ru Date 2026-11-10
Assignment Homework 1 · Literature-Grounded Research Question · Session 1 (Week 1)

Abstract. When investors have bought only a few distinct assets, exact matches on asset categories may
provide little separation among candidates. I propose comparing frozen Qwen3 embeddings with one-hot
encoding of the same four metadata fields using a shared cosine ranker. A positive mean paired nDCG@10
difference with a 95% confidence interval above zero would support the planned comparison in the
one-to-three-asset cohort. The experiment estimates whether changing the asset representation helps predict
future purchases in FAR-Trans.

1. Introduction
With a short purchase history, a recommender must rank many assets using only a few examples of what the
investor bought. For example, a user with one renewable-utility stock may later buy a stock from a related
industry. One-hot encoding gives credit for exact field matches, while a text encoder can also assign similarity
to related labels.

Research importance. Holding the fields and ranker fixed tests whether changing the geometry of asset
similarity adds predictive signal for short histories. The FAR-Trans benchmark found historical popularity hard
to beat [1], so the standalone popularity list gives context for any gain over one-hot encoding.

Business value. A brokerage recommendation product owner could use a reliable lift, together with the
popularity score and measured encoding cost, to decide whether to fund further offline evaluation of an
embedding job. A precisely estimated negligible gain would favor retaining one-hot encoding. Purchase labels
measure behavior, while suitability and investment outcomes require separate evidence [1], [2].

3. Method
Primary research question. We test whether frozen Qwen3 embeddings improve mean nDCG@10 over
one-hot encoding of the same asset metadata for FAR-Trans users who bought one to three distinct assets
before the cutoff.

Raw record and field provenance
The official release [6] contains the following anonymized purchase. Values are verbatim from
FAR-Trans/transactions.csv, CSV line 2 including the header, record 7590224.

  Field                     Verbatim value                    Role and time

  customerID                00017496858921195E5A              Pseudonymous history key, recorded on the transaction
                                                              row.

  ISIN                      GRS434003000                      Asset key for joining and tie-breaking, recorded on the row.

  transactionID             7590224                           Record locator, recorded on the row.

  transactionType           Buy                               Recorded purchase type at the row's transaction date.

  timestamp                 2020-03-27                        Recorded date. Training or evaluation assignment awaits
                                                              the course split.

The archive gives this ISIN a metadata snapshot dated 2018-01-02 with assetCategory = Stock,
assetSubCategory = Large Cap, sector = Utilities and industry = Utilities - Renewable. These are observed
release fields as of the snapshot date. Treat a blank or unavailable field as missing, with the same marker in
both arms. The user representation is derived at the prediction cutoff. Customer profile fields, including
estimated risk or capacity, are excluded. FAR-Trans includes reconstructed transactions [1], so a recorded
date alone does not establish direct observation of the underlying purchase.

  Design element                Specification

  Scope and cohort              Emit a Top-10 list per officially evaluated user. The primary cohort has 1-3 distinct
                                pre-cutoff buy ISINs. Analyze 1, 2 and 3 separately as descriptive slices where counts
                                permit. Ranking predicts purchase behavior. Reranking and investment suitability are
                                outside the study scope.

  Inputs and split              Use only pre-cutoff buys for histories and popularity. Join by ISIN to the latest asset
                                snapshot timestamped at or before the cutoff. Apply the instructor's eligible universe,
                                purchase-label policy, window and treatment of repeat buys once published. Until then
                                these are planning assumptions.

  Baseline and ablation         Concatenate field-specific one-hot vectors for the four fields, including the missing value.
                                Replacing Qwen with one-hot is the encoder ablation. As a standalone reference, rank
                                by pre-cutoff purchase count over the same eligible set.

  Frozen encoder                Use Qwen/Qwen3-Embedding-0.6B [7], revision
                                97b0c614be4d77ee51c0cef4e5f07c00f9eb65b3. Render the four fields in a fixed label order
                                with identical text for history and candidate assets. Cache one embedding per distinct
                                tuple. Use the model in evaluation mode with frozen weights.

  Shared ranking                L2-normalize asset vectors, average the vectors of each user's distinct bought assets,
                                then score eligible assets by cosine similarity. Break ties by higher pre-cutoff popularity,
                                then ascending ISIN. Use popularity for empty histories or zero user vectors. Keep
                                users, labels and candidate rules fixed.




Neklyudov Vladislav · VibeCoding Team 7                                                                                        3
 HSE UNIVERSITY / LLM4REC                                                                       SESSION 1 / REVIEW DRAFT



  Design element                Specification

  Metrics and                   Primary outcome is the mean paired Qwen-minus-one-hot nDCG@10 on the 1-3 cohort,
  uncertainty                   with cohort size and a 95% paired user-bootstrap interval. Report overall scores for all
                                three lists, descriptive subgroup scores, metadata coverage, tie frequency and runtime.

  Compute and schedule          One deterministic run per method on a local workstation and 1,000 bootstrap resamples
                                with seed 42. Use Python, NumPy and Sentence Transformers with versions and
                                hardware logged in Session 2. Budget $0 in paid calls. Target a 30-minute encoding run
                                and estimate it from a 50-tuple pilot before scoring.

  Risks and current state       Use only cutoff-eligible information and keep customer IDs out of model text. Report
                                coverage and provenance checks. The team repo is empty as of 2026-11-10 [8].
                                Session 2 builds the baseline and evaluator. Session 3 runs the encoder and inspects
                                errors. Session 4 packages results, predictions, code and presentation.




Neklyudov Vladislav · VibeCoding Team 7                                                                                    4
 HSE UNIVERSITY / LLM4REC                                                               SESSION 1 / REVIEW DRAFT



4. Experiments
Planned. Run the three methods against identical eligible future-purchase labels, with binary relevance per
distinct purchased asset. Divide the discounted gain of the first ten ranks by the ideal gain for the same user's
eligible positives. Follow the course convention for users without positives. Report the mean per-user score
and, in the primary cohort, bootstrap the paired per-user differences by resampling users. A confidence
interval entirely above zero supports a positive difference. An interval overlapping zero leaves the direction
uncertain unless its width rules out a practically meaningful lift.

Verification plan. In a toy case with one relevant asset at rank two, nDCG@10 is 1/log2(3) ≈ 0.631 because
ideal DCG is 1. Check this case against the evaluator. Verify identical candidate sets, unique Top-10 entries,
deterministic ties, and that no feature timestamps fall after the cutoff. Audit a sample of joins by hand and
report the number of users, eligible assets and missing snapshots. The archive and repository checks inform
this plan. Benchmark measurements are pending.

5. Discussion
Team discussion and individual position. Ivan favored using an LLM to compare each shortlisted asset
directly against the user's purchases. His concern was that averaging could blur distinct interests. Alexander
expected one-hot metadata to be competitive given the coarse taxonomy and concentration of purchases in
popular assets. We agreed to compare frozen Qwen3 with one-hot on the same fields for the
one-to-three-asset cohort, keep the ranker fixed and report popularity separately. Ivan's concern about
averaging and Alexander's expectation about the classical baseline remain open.

As team lead, I wrote the discussion agenda and proposed the encoder swap as the compromise. I favor it
because both encoders face the same limitations of averaging, so a performance difference is interpretable
as an effect of the representation within that ranker. I deferred reranking because introducing a new scoring
procedure would require its own comparison to determine whether it addresses the averaging concern. I kept
popularity because it tests whether either personalized list adds value beyond recommending frequently
bought assets. The question, baseline and reference are shared team decisions.

Interpretation and validity. A positive difference supports this representation for the tested cohort and
cutoff. A narrow interval around zero would constrain the case for paying the extra compute cost. A wide
interval, especially with few eligible users, would leave the effect unresolved. Both encoders assign identical
vectors to identical metadata tuples, so popularity can dominate among tied assets. Report ties and metadata
coverage to show how often the encoder could meaningfully change the ranking.

Market regime, survivorship in the available asset universe, reconstructed transactions and stale metadata
may limit generalization. Stale customer profiles are avoided by excluding profile features. The Qwen

Frozen Asset Embeddings for
Short Purchase Histories in FAR-Trans
Student Neklyudov Vladislav Team VibeCoding Team 7
Email vsneklyudov@edu.hse.ru Date 2026-11-10
Assignment Homework 1 · Literature-Grounded Research Question · Session 1 (Week 1)

Abstract. When investors have bought only a few distinct assets, exact matches on asset categories may
provide little separation among candidates. I propose comparing frozen Qwen3 embeddings with one-hot
encoding of the same four metadata fields using a shared cosine ranker. A positive mean paired nDCG@10
difference with a 95% confidence interval above zero would support the planned comparison in the
one-to-three-asset cohort. The experiment estimates whether changing the asset representation helps predict
future purchases in FAR-Trans.

1. Introduction
With a short purchase history, a recommender must rank many assets using only a few examples of what the
investor bought. For example, a user with one renewable-utility stock may later buy a stock from a related
industry. One-hot encoding gives credit for exact field matches, while a text encoder can also assign similarity
to related labels.

Research importance. Holding the fields and ranker fixed tests whether changing the geometry of asset
similarity adds predictive signal for short histories. The FAR-Trans benchmark found historical popularity hard
to beat [1], so the standalone popularity list gives context for any gain over one-hot encoding.

Business value. A brokerage recommendation product owner could use a reliable lift, together with the
popularity score and measured encoding cost, to decide whether to fund further offline evaluation of an
embedding job. A precisely estimated negligible gain would favor retaining one-hot encoding. Purchase labels
measure behavior, while suitability and investment outcomes require separate evidence [1], [2].




Neklyudov Vladislav · VibeCoding Team 7                                                                       1
 HSE UNIVERSITY / LLM4REC                                                                     SESSION 1 / REVIEW DRAFT

  SIGIR Resource Track,         ranking with advisory dialogues. Uses      dialogue and preference inputs differ from

                                choice-recovery metrics.

  Spadea and                    FLARKO fine-tunes LLMs using               Tests a larger intervention with extra

  ACM ICAIF, 2025               graphs. Tests purchase and profitability   isolate the contribution of a frozen
                                hits at rank 3 on FAR-Trans.               metadata encoder.

  Hou et al. [4]                UniSRec combines item text with a          Motivates semantic item similarity. The
  ACM KDD, 2022                 learned sequence model for                 learned sequence model and
                                cross-domain recommendation on             cross-domain task differ from a fixed
                                Amazon reviews.                            cosine ranker on asset metadata.

  Zhang et al. [5]              Evaluates Qwen3 embedding models on        Supports the checkpoint choice. Its
  arXiv, 2025                   multilingual MTEB and retrieval            benchmarks leave short-history purchase
                                benchmarks.                                prediction open.

Nearest prior work. FAR-Trans [1] answers how several standard methods, including popularity, rank future
purchases under its own protocol. Its comparison leaves open whether semantics from the same four fields
help users with one to three distinct past purchases. A small difference would still bound the incremental gain
from this encoder swap under the course protocol, to the precision the cohort permits.

3. Method
Primary research question. We test whether frozen Qwen3 embeddings improve mean nDCG@10 over
one-hot encoding of the same asset metadata for FAR-Trans users who bought one to three distinct assets
before the cutoff.

Raw record and field provenance
The official release [6] contains the following anonymized purchase. Values are verbatim from
FAR-Trans/transactions.csv, CSV line 2 including the header, record 7590224.

  Field                     Verbatim value                    Role and time

  customerID                00017496858921195E5A              Pseudonymous history key, recorded on the transaction
                                                              row.

  ISIN                      GRS434003000                      Asset key for joining and tie-breaking, recorded on the row.

  transactionID             7590224                           Record locator, recorded on the row.

  transactionType           Buy                               Recorded purchase type at the row's transaction date.

  timestamp                 2020-03-27                        Recorded date. Training or evaluation assignment awaits
                                                              the course split.

The archive gives this ISIN a metadata snapshot dated 2018-01-02 with assetCategory = Stock,
assetSubCategory = Large Cap, sector = Utilities and industry = Utilities - Renewable. These are observed
release fields as of the snapshot date. Treat a blank or unavailable field as missing, with the same marker in
both arms. The user representation is derived at the prediction cutoff. Customer profile fields, including
estimated risk or capacity, are excluded. FAR-Trans includes reconstructed transactions [1], so a recorded
date alone does not establish direct observation of the underlying purchase.

  Design element                Specification

  Scope and cohort              Emit a Top-10 list per officially evaluated user. The primary cohort has 1-3 distinct
                                pre-cutoff buy ISINs. Analyze 1, 2 and 3 separately as descriptive slices where counts
                                permit. Ranking predicts purchase behavior. Reranking and investment suitability are
                                outside the study scope.

  Inputs and split              Use only pre-cutoff buys for histories and popularity. Join by ISIN to the latest asset
                                snapshot timestamped at or before the cutoff. Apply the instructor's eligible universe,
                                purchase-label policy, window and treatment of repeat buys once published. Until then
                                these are planning assumptions.

  Baseline and ablation         Concatenate field-specific one-hot vectors for the four fields, including the missing value.
                                Replacing Qwen with one-hot is the encoder ablation. As a standalone reference, rank
                                by pre-cutoff purchase count over the same eligible set.

  Frozen encoder                Use Qwen/Qwen3-Embedding-0.6B [7], revision
                                97b0c614be4d77ee51c0cef4e5f07c00f9eb65b3. Render the four fields in a fixed label order
                                with identical text for history and candidate assets. Cache one embedding per distinct
                                tuple. Use the model in evaluation mode with frozen weights.

  Shared ranking                L2-normalize asset vectors, average the vectors of each user's distinct bought assets,
                                then score eligible assets by cosine similarity. Break ties by higher pre-cutoff popularity,
                                then ascending ISIN. Use popularity for empty histories or zero user vectors. Keep
                                users, labels and candidate rules fixed.

  Design element                Specification

  Metrics and                   Primary outcome is the mean paired Qwen-minus-one-hot nDCG@10 on the 1-3 cohort,
  uncertainty                   with cohort size and a 95% paired user-bootstrap interval. Report overall scores for all
                                three lists, descriptive subgroup scores, metadata coverage, tie frequency and runtime.

  Compute and schedule          One deterministic run per method on a local workstation and 1,000 bootstrap resamples
                                with seed 42. Use Python, NumPy and Sentence Transformers with versions and
                                hardware logged in Session 2. Budget $0 in paid calls. Target a 30-minute encoding run
                                and estimate it from a 50-tuple pilot before scoring.

  Risks and current state       Use only cutoff-eligible information and keep customer IDs out of model text. Report
                                coverage and provenance checks. The team repo is empty as of 2026-11-10 [8].
                                Session 2 builds the baseline and evaluator. Session 3 runs the encoder and inspects
                                errors. Session 4 packages results, predictions, code and presentation.




Neklyudov Vladislav · VibeCoding Team 7                                                                                    4
 HSE UNIVERSITY / LLM4REC                                                               SESSION 1 / REVIEW DRAFT



4. Experiments
Planned. Run the three methods against identical eligible future-purchase labels, with binary relevance per
distinct purchased asset. Divide the discounted gain of the first ten ranks by the ideal gain for the same user's
eligible positives. Follow the course convention for users without positives. Report the mean per-user score
and, in the primary cohort, bootstrap the paired per-user differences by resampling users. A confidence
interval entirely above zero supports a positive difference. An interval overlapping zero leaves the direction
uncertain unless its width rules out a practically meaningful lift.

Verification plan. In a toy case with one relevant asset at rank two, nDCG@10 is 1/log2(3) ≈ 0.631 because
ideal DCG is 1. Check this case against the evaluator. Verify identical candidate sets, unique Top-10 entries,
deterministic ties, and that no feature timestamps fall after the cutoff. Audit a sample of joins by hand and
report the number of users, eligible assets and missing snapshots. The archive and repository checks inform
this plan. Benchmark measurements are pending.

5. Discussion
Team discussion and individual position. Ivan favored using an LLM to compare each shortlisted asset
directly against the user's purchases. His concern was that averaging could blur distinct interests. Alexander
expected one-hot metadata to be competitive given the coarse taxonomy and concentration of purchases in
popular assets. We agreed to compare frozen Qwen3 with one-hot on the same fields for the
one-to-three-asset cohort, keep the ranker fixed and report popularity separately. Ivan's concern about
averaging and Alexander's expectation about the classical baseline remain open.

As team lead, I wrote the discussion agenda and proposed the encoder swap as the compromise. I favor it
because both encoders face the same limitations of averaging, so a performance difference is interpretable
as an effect of the representation within that ranker. I deferred reranking because introducing a new scoring
procedure would require its own comparison to determine whether it addresses the averaging concern. I kept
popularity because it tests whether either personalized list adds value beyond recommending frequently
bought assets. The question, baseline and reference are shared team decisions.

Interpretation and validity. A positive difference supports this representation for the tested cohort and
cutoff. A narrow interval around zero would constrain the case for paying the extra compute cost. A wide
interval, especially with few eligible users, would leave the effect unresolved. Both encoders assign identical
vectors to identical metadata tuples, so popularity can dominate among tied assets. Report ties and metadata
coverage to show how often the encoder could meaningfully change the ranking.

Market regime, survivorship in the available asset universe, reconstructed transactions and stale metadata
may limit generalization. Stale customer profiles are avoided by excluding profile features. The Qwen

L104: ### 3.1 Prices
L105: 
L106: Prices indicate variations in the value of financial securities. Therefore, the past prices of financial assets represent an important source of information in the development and evaluation of FAR approaches. Pricing time-series have multiple uses: asset analysis through the computation of technical indicators, risk estimation, development of content-based FAR methods or evaluation according to the profitability of assets 【37†Sanz-Cruzado et al. (2022)】.
L107: #### 3.1.1 Cleaning and pre-processing
L108: 
L109: When acquiring pricing data for financial assets, it is not uncommon to find small gaps or invalid values in them caused by problems in the data collection. While these problems are realistic, they add a confounding variable for the asset analysis. Thus, we need to clean and pre-process our data to minimise the impact of these errors.
L110: A potential source of error involves the collection of pricing information from multiple data sources or markets. We clean our dataset so every asset has, at most, a single price value at any given date. We first remove pure duplicates from our data. Then, for those assets that still have multiple values on a date (a) we remove values equal to 0 or (b) we keep the value which is closer to the price of the previous 5 days.
L111: In cases where the price time series changes trading currency mid-day, we keep the value closer to the price of the following 5 days instead (as these days use the new currency).
L112: We next treat major errors within the data: as investment transactions require capital exchange, we removed from our dataset those assets with closing price values equal to 0 at some point in their time series. We also observed assets with time gaps. For shorter periods, we can estimate the missing points, but, the longer the gap, the more inaccurate the estimation will be. We therefore then remove assets with large time gaps (longer than 10 days).
L113: Another aspect to study are sudden variations in price, as they might lead to outliers affecting what FAR algorithms learn. We consider as outliers those values where the price is increased by 10 times or loses 90% of the value on a single day, and price reverts to its original value range on the following day. As those cases are mostly due to errors on data collection, we estimate the correct price by a moving average of the previous five days to prevent undesirable effects.
L114: A more complex case occurs when the price never reverts to its original scale -- as this might reflect a currency change or a stock split. In the first case, we apply price transformations to ensure all time series are represented in euros. In the second case, stock splits represent corporate actions changing the number of shares on which a stock is divided.
L115: For instance, a company might divide every share into two -- causing every investor to own twice the number of shares, but every individual share halved in value. There are two types of splits: direct stock splits increase the number of shares, whereas reverse stock splits diminish it. To prevent variations in our data, we check those assets with increases or decreases of a third of their value in a single day.
L116: Then, with the assistance of Yahoo! Finance^{4}^{4} 4 Yahoo! Finance: 【80†https://finance.yahoo.com/†finance.yahoo.com】, we identify (a) whether a stock split occurred, (b) its date and (c) the split ratio. Then, for every stock split, we divide the prices previous to the split date by the split ratio – for example, if a company performs a 2-for-1 (2:1) stock split, all prices previous to the split date are halved.
L117: Finally, we finish our cleaning process by closing the remaining gaps by applying a moving average over the previous five days.
L118: #### 3.1.2 Statistics
L119: 
L120: Figure 【81†1】(a) illustrates the average price of the assets included in our dataset. As we can observe, our data covers both bullish and bearish market periods – including recent economic recess periods like the Covid-19 pandemic in March 2020, and the effects of the Ukraine-Russian war at the beginning of 2022.
L121: ### 3.2 Assets
L122: 
L123: We collect further information about the financial securities beyond the pricing data. For each of the 807 assets with pricing data, we obtain from public sources their asset type (stock, bond or mutual fund) and sub-type (for instance, bonds can be government or company bonds), their names, the market where they are traded and, where available, their sector and industry.
L124: Figures 【81†1】(b) and (c) provide some statistics about the assets. Figure 【81†1】(b) illustrates the number of assets of each type (stocks, bonds and mutual funds). As it can be observed, the three categories are well represented, with at least 200 assets on each of them – with mutual funds representing the majority of the collection.
L125: Following Figure 【81†1】(c), we also observe that our assets are not just restricted to the Greek market – they represent the assets on which customers could invest through the financial institution. Therefore, although a large fraction of the assets come from Greek markets, there are also assets from other European markets (e.g. Luxembourg and Germany) and some US securities.
L126:  |  |
L127: (a) Average price  | (b) Asset classification by type  | (c) Asset classification by market country
L128: Figure 1: Financial asset statistics.
L129: ### 3.3 Transactions
L130: The main novelty of this dataset is the availability of investment interactions between banking customers and financial assets. These interactions represent acquisitions and sales of the securities by individual investors which have been managed by the financial institution. Investment transactions can be used for modelling the past behaviour of customers and develop personalized recommendation approaches.
L131: They can also be used to evaluate investment prediction using classical recommender systems and information retrieval metrics, which consider these algorithms as a predictor for future customer behaviour 【37†Sanz-Cruzado et al. (2022)】.
L132: #### 3.3.1 Cleaning and pre-processing
L133: The raw data includes customer and asset identifiers, the type (buy, sale) and date of the transaction, the number of shares bought/sold by the investor, the total amount of money involved in the transaction, and the channel the customer used to execute that transaction. However, this raw data needs to be aligned with the rest of the dataset (and, specifically, with the price time series described in Section 【12†3.1】). We therefore perform some cleaning transformations over the initial log.
L134: First, every transaction needs an associated customer to it, so we removed those with a blank customer. Once this is done, we consider the effects that stock splits have on the number of shares every customer owns by multiplying the number of acquired/sold shares by the split ratio.
L135: If a customer owns fractional shares after a reverse stock split, we assume that the company provides cash instead of those fractional shares^{5}^{5} 5 https://finance.yahoo.com/news/why-investors-cash-lieu-fractional-140004745.html and we add a transaction selling those fractional shares at the date of the split.
L136: Another observation over the raw data is that customers sell assets which they never acquired during the 2018-2022 period, indicating that they acquired them earlier and had them in their portfolio. To ensure that every asset sale is backed by a purchase, we recreate those asset buys. For every customer, we compute the number of shares she owns of every asset.
L137: If the investor owns a negative number of shares (meaning that she has sold more shares than she has bought) at the end of 2022, we add a buy transaction at the earliest point in time for which we have pricing data for the asset (in a majority of cases, 2nd January 2018). We assume that the customer acquires the number of shares which were sold in excess.
L138: Afterwards, we fix those cases where customers interact with assets at times when the pricing data is not available. In case the transaction is outside the range of dates for which we have pricing data, we move the transaction to the closest date where the price exists. Then, we check if customers have shares of an asset after the end of the pricing time series of the security. If they do, we add a transaction selling those assets.
L139: Finally, we solve inconsistencies on asset prices by providing an estimate of the total value of the transaction. We estimate the value by multiplying the number of shares by the closing price of the asset on the date of the transaction. In the end, we have 388,049 transactions in our dataset, corresponding to 29,090 customers.
L140: #### 3.3.2 Statistics
L141: 
L142:  |  |
L143: (a) Transaction distribution over time  | (b) Customer transaction distribution  | (c) Asset transaction distribution
L144: Figure 2: Transaction statistics.
L145: We summarize in Figure 【82†2】 the statistics of the transaction data. First, 【82†2】(a) displays the number of investment transactions registered on every month of the studied period. In the figure, the $x$ axis shows the dates, whereas the $y$ axis represents the number of transactions. The green line represents the asset purchases, the red line represents the sales and the blue line represents the combined number of transactions.
L146: The first observation from this figure is that most of the transactions occur in the period between January 2020 and November 2022, with over 5,000 interactions happening every month. The previous period, between January 2018 and December 2019 only receives between 1,000 and 2,000 trades per month, with the exception of January 2018.
L147: However, the large number of transactions at that date is due to the creation of asset buys representing what customers had in their portfolio before the beginning of the period covered by our dataset. The actual largest number of transactions occurs in March 2020, corresponding with the time the Covid-19 pandemic hit Europe, likely due to the huge drop in market prices that occurred during that period.
L148: Figures 【82†2】(b) and (c) represent, respectively, the transaction distribution over customers and assets. The $y$ axis represents the number of customers/assets which have associated the number of transactions as indicated on the $x$ axis. Due to the skewness of the distributions, we represent both figures in log-log scale.
L149: The investment distribution by customers in Figure 【82†2】(b) resembles a long-tail distribution, where a majority of customers only modify their portfolios a few times over the whole period (over 50% of the users have 3 or less transactions between 2018 and 2022) whereas only a few customers modify their investments continuously (around 650 customers have more than 100 transactions). This long-tail distribution is similar to other recommender system datasets like MovieLens.
L150: A different pattern is observed when we examine the asset distribution however. First, as indicated in Table 【79†1】, less than half of the assets (321 out of 807) have ever been bought or sold in our dataset.
L151: Second, although the distribution illustrated in Figure 【82†2】 is skewed, this is due to a few assets concentrating lots of transactions: even when most of the interacted assets have a reasonable number of transactions (75% of them have more than 20 interactions, and 58% of them have more than 100), the top 12 assets concentrate more than 50% of the dataset interactions. This indicates that there is an important popularity factor over the collected transactions.
L152: ### 3.4 Customers
L153: Financial asset recommendation needs to consider the specific needs and preferences of the customers. However, all that information is not only hidden in the past customer transactions: explicit information about customer investment capacity or risk profile can be considered to identify more relevant investment opportunities for retail customers. As such, we include in the dataset information about the classification of customers within the bank, their investment risk profile and their investment capacity.
L154: We collect that information from the 29,090 customers within the bank who have, at least, one investment reflected in our cleaned transaction data. All customer information has been thoroughly anonymized and does not contain sensitive data to satisfy regulations. We provide further descriptions for the customer classifications below:
L155:  |  |
L156: (a) Customer classification by segment  | (b) Customer classification by risk profile  | (c) Customer classification by capacity
L157: Figure 3: Customer statistics.
L158: #### 3.4.1 Customer segments
L159: 
L160: Customer segments represent the internal classification of customers within the bank. We consider five different segments in our data:
L161: 
L162:   * •
L163: 
L164: Mass: The majority of the customers. This category represents customers with less than €60,000 of managed assets (investments, deposits and insurance products).
L165: 
L166:   * •
L167: 
L168: Premium: Individual customers with more than €60,000 on managed assets.
L169: 
L170:   * •
L171: Professional: Sole proprietorship. Individual customer exercising their activity without having created a legal person.
L172: 
L173:   * •
L174: 
L175: Legal Entitiy: This category represents legal entities with services within the bank.
L176: 
L177:   * •
L178: 
L179: Inactive: Customers without available segment.
L180: Figure 【83†3】(a) shows the distribution of customers over the different categories: as we can observe individual retail investors represent the majority of the dataset, with 18,610 mass customers, 8,906 premium customers, followed by the business customers (1,327 professional and 39 legal entities). The segment of 208 customers remains unknown.
L181: #### 3.4.2 Investment risk profile
L182: The investment risk profile categorises customers according to the amount of risk they would accept on their investments. To assess if the offered investment assets are suitable for their investment goals and aligned with their risk aversion, every customer who is interested in investing is asked by the bank to complete an investment profile questionnaire with 25 questions. We provide these questions on the dataset.
L183: Following the MiFID II 【84†Council (2014)】 regulatory framework, this risk assessment aims to ensure that the financial instruments provided to investors are compatible with their needs, characteristics and goals. According to their answers, their risk profile in one of the following four categories:
L184:   * •
L185: 
L186: Conservative: Conservative customers prioritize protecting their capital. Their portfolios should be easily liquidated and present extremely low investment risk. An example portfolio might include short-term placements and fixed-income securities.
L187: 
L188:   * •
L189: 
L190: Income: Customers with this risk profile aim at generating a fixed income arising from bond coupons, dividends and short-term placements. Their portfolios should present very low investment risk.
L191: 
L192:   * •
L193: Balanced: Accepting possible fluctuations on the invested capital, these customers aim at generating fixed income from coupons and dividends, as well as medium-term capital gains. An example portfolio would contain both bonds and stocks.
L194: 
L195:   * •
L196: 
L197: Aggressive: This profile aims at significant long-term gains, which come with high risks.
L198: The risk profile is precise for those customers who have already answered the questionnaire. In case they have not, the score is simulated through an automated process: first, given the answered questionnaires, linear regression is used to determine which questions have the largest weight. Then, estimations for the most important scores are obtained from alternative customer data (e.g., yearly salary estimation).
L199: Using estimations on those basic components and their weights, it is possible to simulate the risk tolerance for those customers without questionnaires. A risk profile is estimated following this method for 7,141 investors in our dataset.
L200: Figure 【83†3】(b) displays the distribution of customers according to their investment risk profiling. We find that most customers favor intermediate risk profiles (income and balanced), with a minority willing to risk their capital on aggressive investments.
L201: #### 3.4.3 Investment capacity
L202: The last customer categorization divides customers by the amount of money they can invest: we consider four different segments according to their investment limit: (a) less than €30,000, (b) between €30,000 and €80,000, (b) between €80,000 and €300,000 and (d) more than €300,000. These values are obtained from the risk assessment questionnaire. A similar procedure to the one used for risk profile is used for those customers without assessment (in this case, this is estimated for 7,318 customers).
L203: The customer distribution is illustrated in Figure 【83†3】(c). In that figure, we can observe that a majority of the investors in our dataset have a low investment capacity (less than €30k). This is consistent with our customer segmentation, where more than 18,000 customers were identified as mass customers, with less than €60k on investments.
L204: The number of customers in each category diminishes as the investment capacity increases (with those customers capable of investments above €300k representing a minority of the dataset).
